HEADLINE: Democracy never part of deal: Ex-envoy
TEXT:
Canberra | Australia's engagement with China over the past 40 years has not been a failure, despite China's failure to liberalise politically as it got richer, former ambassador to China Geoff Raby says.

In an opinion piece for The Australian Financial Review's "Australia's China Challenge" series, Mr Raby writes that Australian policymakers never carried the same "ideological baggage" as the US when China began opening up in the 1970s.

"Among the many things China is accused of today is that it did not live up to its side of an implicit bargain with the West to become a liberal democracy and a fully paid-up member of the US-led international order in return for the West's welcoming China into the international system after decades of isolation, obscurity and stagnation," he writes.

"Australia was among the first in the OECD to recognise the profound potential of China's early reforms to transform the country economically, creating enormous opportunity for Australia as a result.

"Far from buyers' remorse, it has proved to be an outstandingly successful investment for Australia. China's becoming like us was never part of the bargain," he writes.

However, Peter Jennings, Australian Strategic Policy Institute chief, disputes this. He says it was "frankly ridiculous" to suggest Canberra's engagement with China was focused purely on maximising economic gains, without reference to Australian values such as respect for rule of law and free speech.

"If that was the case we might as well trade with North Korea," he said.

"Really from the moment that China was brought into the World Trade Organisation there was an assumption that wealth would gradually make China more open - maybe not more democratic, but we would see trappings of a free press and people willing to speak their mind. The comment was it would become more like Singapore.

"We were doing so much on the premise of what China was meant to be. It was a failure of a generation of policymakers, of which Raby was part," Mr Jennings said.

Former prime minister John Howard predicted in a 2012 speech given just six weeks before Xi Jinping became head of the Chinese Communist Party that "pressure for more democracy in China will grow".

"I find it difficult to accept that growing economic liberalism will continue to walk hand in hand with political authoritarianism," Mr Howard said when delivering the Sir John Downer Oration.

"The first newly enriched generation may accept authority, but their children will take affluence for granted and demand more say in running their own lives."

Mr Howard, like many in the West, has become less confident of Chinese reforms, earlier this year labelling Mr Xi more of a "bully" than his predecessors. However, he maintains Australia's end game must be to have as big an economic relationship as possible with China.

Mr Raby argues Australia had three objectives: encourage China to open its markets to the world to expand economic opportunities; expect prosperity to make China more settled politically with its neighbours; and mitigate the risk that a collapse in Chinese order would drive out millions of refugees.

Australia-China Relations Institute head James Laurenceson backed Mr Raby's assessment, saying China's culture and history made it unlikely to embrace Western liberalism.

However, he said China had become a "responsible stakeholder" in many areas, citing as one example its role with Australia and 18 other countries to set up an alternative trade dispute mechanism at the World Trade Organisation after the US forced the appellate body to shut down.

"The idea that China would just become like us because it became richer was nonsensical," he said.

"There are certainly problems with China's current authoritarian bent, but a stable, prosperous China is in Australia's interest, both economically and also strategically."

HEADLINE: ANZ changing work for staff stuck at home
TEXT:
Shorter meetings with fewer people and junking reports to use live dashboards are some of the many ways ANZ Bank is adapting to a second lockdown of Victoria and its staff.

ANZ's group executive for retail and commercial banking Mark Hand said although the shift to working from home had some advantages, predictions for employers such as ANZ to require much less office space in future were wide of the mark.

"I think the forecasts are wrong that people will require less office space. Employees will continue to social distance. Some will continue to work from home but others enjoy the interaction. Humans like routine," he said.

Mr Hand was among the first cohort of the bank's employees to begin working from home, allowing him identify problems and iron out kinks early on.

Prohibited from printing out work documents at home, ANZ staff have replaced many of the monthly and quarterly reports with dashboards that can be updated regularly, leading to a big shift in the way metrics are reported and distributed.

"I haven't printed a single sheet of paper since March 10," Mr Hand said. The daunting daily schedule of Zoom meetings has likewise been optimised. Meetings previously booked for an hour run no longer than 45 minutes, agenda items are clearly defined and attendees are all genuine stakeholders, not just interested onlookers. "We have less people in meetings, shorter meetings, clearer agendas and much clearer communication," he said.

While some aspects of the bank's business have been made more efficient thanks to COVID-19, the task of managing large numbers of employees has not been made any easier.

As the head of the bank's Australian operations, Mr Hand is responsible for more than 12,000 employees, making one-on-one chats impossible. The bank does, however, hold weekly catch-ups with CEO Shayne Elliot and Mr Hand speaks to his executive team of 800 once a fortnight.

"We have to make sure the mental well-being of our staff is top of mind," he said. "It can be quite tough, reminding them to stay focused but also that they can't be sitting at their desk all day. We want staff to get outside and walk and talk when they can."

Like many other large corporations, ANZ now has many staff who have never met their managers face-to-face because of COVID-19. Mr Hand said this was a particular concern when it came to the bank's graduate intake who typically require more attention than an experienced banker.

"These are young, talented and ambitious people who have never had a chat about their career," Mr Hand said. "It's harder because you might have never met them. It's definitely different and less obvious, so we are working to adapt and give them forums to raise questions."

Echoing similar statements by ANZ Bank chairman David Gonski last week, Mr Hand said it was important managers did not project their own idyllic work-from-home scenarios on to others. He said the bank was aware of the challenges employees with families or singles were grappling with.

"I know a couple of single parents who are recently separated and in smaller accommodation than they are used to," he said. "They're home schooling two kids at the kitchen table and have their laptop sitting on an ironing board. Now, I can sit in my office and say 'This is not too bad', but you've always got to remember that some are living in shared accommodation where it's difficult to get time alone to work or concentrate."

Making yourself available outside regular working hours was one way of making things easier for your staff, Mr Hand said. But the downside was that management was spread more thinly over a longer day.

Like many executives, he admits to having some difficulty switching off. Mr Hand said foreign films or co-productions with subtitles were one way to stop multi-tasking.

When asked whether working from home had led to a slide in dress standards across the bank, the crisply dressed Mr Hand confessed while his personal style veered towards the smarter end of smart casual, things had taken a turn in recent weeks.

"I have started to see a few hoodies creep in but it's been pretty good up until now," he said.

HEADLINE: Financial Review posts strongest readership growth
TEXT:
The Australian Financial Review has posted the strongest annual audience growth among national, Sydney and Melbourne newspaper mastheads by retaining most of the initial surge of readership sparked by the COVID-19 crisis.

The Financial Review posted 26 per cent growth in digital and print readership in the year to June, outstripping gains by News Corp rivals The Australian, Sydney's Daily Telegraph and Melbourne's The Herald Sun as well as its Nine stablemates The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age.

The Financial Review reinforced its rise to become Australia's sixth-most read newspaper title.

The Sydney Morning Herald retains the biggest newspaper masthead audience by far, boasting almost 9.4 million digital and print readers in June.

Previously, the national business, finance and political daily's digital and print audience jumped more than 50 per cent, or almost 1.3 million Financial Review readers, in the three months to March, when the coronavirus crisis hit.

Over the following three months, the masthead held onto more than two-thirds of that bigger audience to record more than 3.3 million readers in June, up from almost 2.7 million a year before, according to the latest three-monthly survey by Enhanced Media Metrics Australia.

Overall, the Financial Review has recorded a slight fall in print readership in the past year, which was more than offset by a 42 per cent jump in digital audience, according to the EMMA survey.

That amounted to an extra 676,000 readers overall in the 12 months to June.

The Financial Review's editor-in-chief, Michael Stutchbury, said the shift to working from home, rather than at the office, had translated into a stepped-up jump in the number of premium digital subscribers.

"It is reassuring to have held onto most of the extra readers who turned to the Financial Review during the uncertainty and fear of March and April when the number of COVID-19 cases jumped, dole queues appeared, the sharemarket slump bottomed and the federal government, the Reserve Bank and the private banks implemented unprecedented income support and loan repayment holidays," he said.

The Financial Review would upgrade its digital coverage through last week's appointment of Fiona Buffini to the new position of deputy editor (digital), he said.

Stutchbury said the acceleration of the audience shift to digital revealed continuing demand for traditional news curation and editing.

This was shown by the popularity of email newsletters and the increased online and app viewing of "today's paper", just as it looked in print.

Although COVID-19 had forced many glossy magazines to close permanently, readership of the inserted monthly The Australian Financial Review Magazine had increased 11 per cent over the year to June to 166,000 readers, he said.

HEADLINE: Virus victims lawyer up in Victoria
TEXT:
It didn't take long for the COVID-19 class action suits to start. Quinn Emanuel, one of the legal firms prominent in the class action industry, is seeking compensation on behalf of businesses that have suffered losses due to the Victorian government's mishandling of hotel quarantine.

This is the first class action lawsuit filed over Victoria's disastrous use of private security guards. It certainly won't be the last. Given the extent of financial devastation facing Victorian businesses, the amount of potential compensation sought is almost beyond comprehension. Caveat Victorian taxpayer. Other law firms are circling, lured by the prospect of more lucrative class actions.

At least two more suits have been filed against the operators of aged care facilities in Victoria, including the now infamous St Basil's, for example.

Yet whatever the merits of individual class actions, they have already combined into one of Australia's most successful growth industries in recent years - with this country an international hotspot because of the relative ease of filing and the big dollars involved.

The actions are usually backed by litigation funders, many global, that take a generous percentage share of the spoils - often tens of millions of dollars - in return for money to run the case. More than 30 are operating in Australia.

Now this will inevitably become a major issue for all Victorians as well. Revelations of the government's bungling of a hotel quarantine program that created Victoria's second wave are fertile territory for any class action lawyer. The inquiry set up by the government may have delayed political reckoning for the Andrews government but could eventually provide the evidence to help cripple it financially.

"This will be Victoria's version of a Clive Palmer $30 billion claim against the Western Australian government," says one legal expert.

In Quinn Emanuel's case, the lead plaintiff is a Melbourne burger restaurant but the suit is open to other businesses in Victoria on July 1 whose ability to supply customers was adversely affected by the stage three and four lockdowns that began in early July.

Line up, line up, one and all.

With Premier Daniel Andrews ruling out any timetable for reopening the state despite mounting federal government pressure, possibilities for class action suits to recover some of the billions of dollars of damage done seem more endless than the lockdown itself.

The other distinction in this case was that it was filed in the Victorian Supreme Court just ahead of the deadline for the introduction of new rules and requirements for litigation funders that took effect on August 22. Labor will try to persuade crossbenchers to help block these regulations in the Senate this week, using the dubious argument they "restrict access to justice".

The government argues that Labor is really more interested in promoting "vested interests" - including those of the leading Labor-aligned law firms involved in class actions such as Maurice Blackburn and Slater & Gordon.

The Victorian government has already recently made it possible for legal firms to operate on a contingency fee basis rather one limited to charging fees as in all other states.

This is likely to make class actions filed in Victoria even more financially appealing. Quinn Emanuel, a US-based law firm, is running the COVID case on a contingency fee basis, for example, backed by money from Regency Funding, an Australian company ultimately owned by a US entity and with two of its three directors in Texas.

Despite the unpredictability of the Senate, the government is confident it can persuade enough crossbenchers to head off Labor's assault on litigation funding regulation.

After all, the changes only require litigation funders to hold an Australian Financial Services Licence and classify them as managed investment schemes.

This licence includes the obligation to act "efficiently honestly and fairly" and in the best interests of class members, while a managed investment scheme requires fuller disclosure of legal costs and commissions being paid.

The combined impact of litigation funding percentages and legal fees means the members of the class action receive, on average, only just over half of any money awarded as compensation according to the Australian Law Reform Commission.

Treasurer Josh Frydenberg could not see any reason to further delay closing the loopholes for litigation funders by waiting for the report of the current parliamentary inquiry due this year.

According to Innes Willox of the Australian Industry Group, the regulations are long overdue.

"Litigation funders should be regulated like any other business which offers financial services," he wrote in a letter to crossbenchers last week. "The level of returns that some funders are currently earning are egregious and some of their practices are unacceptable."

According to legal publication Lawyerly, the imposition of these rules was enough to ensure a rush to file 11 class action lawsuits just ahead of the August deadline - mostly shareholder class actions against companies ranging from CBA to Boral to AMP to CIMIC.

Labor's attempt to thwart the new regulations is backed by a class action lobby group and ad campaign - Keep Corporations Honest - spearheaded by Slater & Gordon.

But Omni Bridgeway, the huge ASX-listed litigation funder formerly known as IMF Bentham, backs greater regulation of the industry in Australia. Omni Bridgeway operates several funds attracting investors, mostly from offshore, with a minimum $25 million to spend and has funded 78 class actions.

Chief executive Andrew Saker supports the need for both an Australian Financial Services Licence and application of the managed investment scheme regime with modifications.

In his view, this will increase public confidence in litigation funding.

Just what a coming rash of COVID-19 claims against the Victorian government will do to public confidence is far more complicated.
